title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Balance register-file reads with shared one-hot address decoding
motivation:
The bench register file implements two asynchronous reads using variable
array indexing, followed by write-first bypass and x0 selection. These
32-bit read paths feed ID/EX every cycle and expose wide address-controlled
multiplexers to FPGA synthesis. Shared address decoding and parallel data
selection offer a localized opportunity to improve timing without adding
pipeline cycles. The only recorded bench experiment is the baseline retest:
127.03 MHz median Fmax, 9563 LUT4s, 4491485 bracketed CoreMark cycles, and
282.82 iterations/sec. LESSONS.md is absent and there are no prior read-path
attempts in the bench log. No detailed timing report is available, so the
register file is a candidate bottleneck, not a confirmed critical path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rewrite only the combinational read implementation in rtl/reg_file.sv.
For each read port, decode its five-bit address once into mutually exclusive
selects for x1 through x31, shared across all 32 data bits. AND-mask each
stored word with its select and combine the terms with an explicitly
balanced OR reduction tree rather than a serial accumulation or a priority
mux. Supply a zero leaf for x0 so reading x0 always returns zero.

Include the existing write-first bypass as an exclusive parallel data term:
bypass = w_en && (read_addr != 0) && (w_addr == read_addr). When bypass is
true, suppress all stored-word selects and select w_data; otherwise select
exactly the addressed stored word. Preserve the current synchronous write
and reset behavior, two independent combinational read ports, module ports,
and all architectural register values. Add no pipeline state or latency.

The intended benefit is less serial mux logic on the register-file read
paths and better sharing of address decode logic across data bits. With
unchanged cycle-level behavior, any median Fmax gain translates directly
into the same percentage fitness gain. The estimate is 5 percent with
medium confidence; decode fanout, routing congestion, or a critical path
elsewhere could erase the gain. Validate existing register-file and
pipeline tests, formal and stalled cosim, then compare the unchanged
three-seed FPGA fitness evaluation against 282.82. Preserve nret=1, all
RVFI and bus-handshake semantics, decoder legality, and every eval check.

Preserve storage, synchronous reset and write behavior, and zero-cycle

title: Single pending-store slot with direct zero-wait completion
motivation:
In cores/bench, hazard_unit freezes IF, ID, and EX whenever a memory
instruction in EX/MEM encounters io_dmemReady=0. An aligned RAM store
already has its address, data, and byte enables at this point, so retaining
those fields separately can release the pipeline to execute younger
arithmetic while the write waits for the bus. This directly targets the
approximately 22% random data-bus backpressure used for CoreMark fitness.

Bench has no LESSONS.md and its experiment log contains only the baseline:
4,491,485 timed cycles and 127.03 MHz median Fmax, yielding 282.82 iter/s.
Read-only reference evidence from cores/v1, hyp-20260428-017-r8s1, supports
a single pending store with a direct ready path: it passed formal/cosim
and improved fitness 5.89% on that different design. Its cycle saving was
under 1%, and placement contributed to the result, so that improvement
must not be assumed for bench. The main risk is losing more Fmax to bus
arbitration than the saved stall cycles recover.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Decouple store retirement from bus completion with exactly one pending
store slot. Allocate it only for a valid, legal, naturally aligned store
whose complete access lies in normal RAM [0x00000000, 0x00100000), when
the slot is empty and io_dmemReady=0. Capture the effective byte address,
existing replicated write data, and byte mask atomically. Advance that
instruction into MEM/WB once, carrying its original PC, instruction,
operands, and aligned RVFI memory fields. Its eventual bus drain produces
no additional retirement. The slot holds only the physical write request;
RVFI metadata continues along the existing pipeline.

With the slot empty and io_dmemReady=1, loads and stores use the existing
direct MEM path without an enqueue cycle. While the slot is valid, give
its request sole ownership of dmem, hold address/data/byte enables stable
until a ready handshake, and suppress any younger external request.
Drain independently of frontend stalls and redirects. Permit younger
non-memory instructions to advance and retire in order while it drains.
Block every younger load or store until the slot is empty, including the
cycle that drains the old request; omit simultaneous drain/refill,
coalescing, and store-to-load forwarding to keep arbitration small.

All MMIO, UART, start/stop marker accesses, and out-of-range addresses
remain on the existing unbuffered path. Never use buffering to hide an
out-of-bounds access from the existing checks. FENCE/FENCE.I, EBREAK,
and trapping instructions must also wait for an older pending store to
drain. Marker writes complete only on their real bus handshake, after
prior writes, so the timed region cannot exclude undrained work. Invalid,
illegal, and misaligned stores never enqueue or drive a write. Redirects
cannot discard an already accepted older store; reset clears slot validity.

Replace the hazard unit's raw dmem-stall predicate with a MEM-generated
mem_wait signal describing whether the current EX/MEM instruction can
advance. A pending store alone must not assert mem_wait for arithmetic.
On a real wait, preserve the existing EX/MEM and ID/EX holds and the
MEM/WB behavior that clears valid but retains forwarding data. Derive
mem_wait from current registered state, instruction classification, and
bus readiness, without a combinational dependency on hold_wb. Keep the
direct zero-wait path short and retain the existing EX datapath and
load-use interlock. Preserve nret=1, all top-level ports, strict channel-0
retirement order, decoder legality, and every existing correctness gate.

Success requires a measured fitness improvement over 282.82 using the
unchanged marker-bracketed CoreMark run and three-seed median Fmax. The
estimate is a 2% fitness gain from overlapping store waits with useful
execution while keeping Fmax close to baseline; it is not a measured
result. Verify the pending path with directed and random bus stalls,
since a ready-tied-high formal configuration cannot exercise allocation.

title: Small tagged target predictor with two-bit branch hysteresis
motivation:
The bench core always fetches PC+4 and redirects in EX for every taken
conditional branch, JAL, and JALR. Its IF/ID bundle is combinational, so
each such redirect discards one younger issue slot, not two registered
frontend stages. Predicting recurring taken transfers can remove that
bubble. A small PC-indexed target table avoids adding instruction-memory
decode and a branch-immediate adder to the fetch-to-PC path. The target
has no LESSONS.md and its experiment log contains only the 282.82 baseline;
there is no recorded predictor attempt to repeat or rule out.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one 16-entry direct-mapped branch target predictor inside if_stage.
Index by PC[5:2]; each entry stores valid, the full remaining PC tag
PC[31:6], an aligned target[31:2], and a two-bit saturating counter.
A valid tag hit with counter[1] set predicts the stored target; otherwise
predict PC+4. This is 944 bits of table state before synthesis. Use a
combinational lookup and synchronous updates, with no same-cycle update
bypass. Reset all valid bits and mask invalid payloads from predictions.
Do not specialize addresses or instruction sequences to CoreMark.

Train exactly once when a valid EX instruction advances: in.valid &&
!stall && !reset. A legal, nontrapping taken conditional branch allocates
a missing entry at 2'b10 or increments a matching entry, and writes its
resolved aligned target. A legal JAL/JALR writes its resolved target and
counter 2'b11; JALR uses the last resolved target without a return stack.
A legal not-taken conditional branch decrements a matching counter without
replacing its target and does not allocate on a miss. Invalidate a matching
entry when that PC resolves to a non-control instruction or a trap. Keep
prediction entirely advisory and preserve full architectural addresses.

Carry the exact predicted next PC selected for each accepted instruction
through IF/ID and ID/EX. In EX, compute actual_next_pc using the existing
forwarded operands and misalignment rules, including PC+4 on the existing
trap path. Redirect only when a valid advancing instruction's actual next
PC differs from its recorded prediction. Compare for every instruction,
so stale entries on non-branches and taken-to-taken JALR target changes
recover correctly. Feed actual_next_pc, never the prediction, into RVFI.

A prediction advances the PC only when ID accepts that fetch; load-use,
instruction-bus, and data-bus stalls must not consume a prediction.
EX recovery overrides an instruction-bus stall. Defer recovery and table
training while EX is held by a data-bus stall, then resolve once on release.
Reuse the existing hazard flush path for mispredictions; a correct taken
prediction must not flush the fetched target instruction. Preserve the
existing MEM/WB forwarding retention, trap behavior, and nret=1 interface.

Expect an approximately eight percent net fitness improvement from fewer
control-transfer bubbles, with medium confidence because table conflicts
and added lookup/recovery logic may offset the cycle savings through Fmax.
Validate with the unchanged correctness gates and bracketed, stalled
CoreMark run; compare median three-seed Fmax times iterations/cycle against
282.82 and report LUT/FF growth. This estimate is not a measured result.

implementation_notes:
Implemented the 16-entry direct-mapped target predictor in `cores/bench/rtl/if_stage.sv`: PC[5:2] index, full PC[31:6] tag, aligned target[31:2], two-bit saturating counter, and one valid bit per entry (944 table bits before synthesis). Only valid tag hits with counter[1] set predict a target. Payloads are not reset; reset clears every valid bit. Lookup is combinational, updates are synchronous, and there is no update bypass or instruction-memory decode in the lookup.

Training is qualified by `in.valid && !stall && !reset` in EX. Taken conditional branches allocate weakly taken or increment a matching counter and update the target; not-taken branches decrement only matching entries and retain their target. Legal JAL/JALR train strongly taken with the last resolved target. Non-control instructions and traps invalidate matching entries. No addresses or instruction sequences are specialized to CoreMark.

IF/ID and ID/EX carry the exact selected 32-bit predicted next PC. EX compares it with the resolved architectural next PC for every advancing instruction, including non-control instructions, illegal instructions, misaligned transfers, and changing JALR destinations. RVFI receives only the architectural next PC. Recovery uses the existing hazard flush path, overrides instruction-bus stalls, and is deferred during data-bus stalls. Correct predictions do not flush the target. MEM/WB forwarding retention, link writes, JALR bit-zero clearing, trap behavior, and the complete external nret=1 port declaration are preserved.

Small implementation deviations: the hazard unit's unchanged equations are expressed as separate continuous assignments to eliminate false combinational-loop warnings in the cocotb build with public signal visibility. A guarded core_pkg.sv include makes the requested alphabetical-glob lint command work as well as the existing package-first builds. Added `test_if_stage.py` for direct lookup/update timing and reset checks, in addition to the requested pipeline tests.

The pipeline harness now uses deterministic bus-ready schedules and applies stores only on accepting clock edges. Every run checks strict RVFI order increments, exact PC-to-next-PC chaining, and one-to-one agreement between bus stores and retired stores. Added coverage for cold/warm backward loops and exits, forward taken branches, direct jumps, changing load-dependent JALR targets, full high address tags and targets, conflicting indices, counter hysteresis, reset, stale non-control/illegal/misaligned instructions, prediction stalls, recovery during instruction stalls, and an EX branch held behind a stalled load using retained MEM/WB forwarding. The held-branch test verifies that a single taken resolution trains once, rather than saturating during the hold.

Local correctness status:

- Required `verilator --lint-only -Wall -Wno-MULTITOP -sv +incdir+cores/bench/rtl cores/bench/rtl/*.sv`: PASS, no warnings. Also passed with `--public-flat-rw`.
- `bash formal/run_all.sh` with `RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench`: PASS, 53 passed / 0 failed, including on the final source. The script automatically selected the nret=1 wrapper/config. No formal counterexamples or formal fix attempts were needed. This is the unchanged ALTOPS gate.
- Full cocotb suite: PASS, 6 pytest runners / 93 cocotb tests, including 24 pipeline and 2 predictor unit tests.
- Unchanged `tools.eval.cosim` gate: PASS, selftest RVFI comparison and bracketed stalled CoreMark CRC validation (2 ELFs).
- Warm backward-loop branch-to-target retirement gaps: 2 cycles for the cold taken branch, then 1 cycle for each warm taken branch; the loop exit costs 2 cycles. A warm self-JAL retires every cycle.
- External core port declaration matches the baseline exactly; all RTL/test files in the validation copy match the delivered source.

All build, formal, synthesis, and simulation artifacts were staged under `$TMPDIR/hyp-20260905-003-r1s2-validation`. The gate scripts, wrappers, reference model, and benchmark sources were copied without modification. The source worktree changes are limited to bench RTL/tests and this requested notes file.

The prompt's 6 KB description differs from the checked-in fitness contract: `bench/programs/Makefile` defaults to TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=2000, and `tools/eval/fpga.py` requires the 2 KB CRCs. Both configurations were exercised without changing either contract file. The comparable score against the recorded 282.82 baseline uses the unchanged 2 KB gate. The separate requested 6 KB build uses TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=6000, -O3, and ITERATIONS=10.

The 6 KB final-source simulation completed under `--bench --istall --dstall`, with no out-of-bounds access. Markers were start=53,747 and stop=30,876,867, giving 30,823,120 measured cycles. It reported crclist=0xd4b0, crcmatrix=0xbe52, crcstate=0x5e47, crcfinal=0x5949, and the literal "Correct operation validated." The UART's size field is per algorithm; its compiler-flags string is hardcoded in the unchanged port, while the actual build command used -O3.

Final-source synthesis and all three unchanged nextpnr seed runs passed. Fmax for seeds 1/2/3 was 134.68 / 141.88 / 127.71 MHz; the median is 134.68 MHz. The unchanged stalled 2 KB gate measured 4,215,937 bracketed cycles for 10 iterations, or approximately 2.371952e-6 iterations/cycle. Fitness is computed from that full-precision ratio, rather than the evaluator's rounded `ipc_coremark` display.

| Metric | Recorded baseline | Final predictor | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Fitness (iterations/s) | 282.82 | 319.45 | +12.95% |
| Median Fmax (MHz) | 127.03 | 134.68 | +6.02% |
| Bracketed cycles | 4,491,485 | 4,215,937 | -6.14% |
| LUT4 | 9,563 | 10,645 | +1,082 (+11.31%) |
| FF | 1,866 | 2,075 | +209 (+11.20%) |

At the same measured median Fmax, the separate 6 KB run corresponds to 43.69 iterations/s. The recorded 282.82 baseline belongs to the checked-in 2 KB gate, so it is not a like-for-like baseline for that 6 KB result.

The measured final-source improvement exceeds the hypothesis's estimated eight percent. Area growth and the spread between placement seeds remain costs/uncertainties; this local result does not replace the orchestrator's independent acceptance run. The final measurement above supersedes the preliminary measurement taken before the hazard-equation cleanup. Evidence is in the scratch copy's `cores/bench/generated/fitness-final.json`, `formal-final.log`, `unit-tests.log`, `cosim-result.json`, `coremark-6k-final.log`, and `pnr_seed{1,2,3}/nextpnr.log`.
lesson: - 2026-09-05 hyp-20260905-003-r1s2 (improvement, +12.95%): A 16-entry tagged target predictor removes the combinational IF/ID frontend's one-slot EX redirect bubble on correctly predicted taken branches/jumps, cutting stalled CoreMark cycles 6.14% while median Fmax rose 6.02%, at about 11% LUT/FF growth.

title: Register one-hot ALU operation selects before execute
motivation:
The current bench winner reaches 319.45 iterations/sec at 134.68 MHz
median Fmax. Its saved final nextpnr reports, whose validation-copy RTL
matches the current bench RTL byte-for-byte, identify a concrete control
timing bottleneck: seeds 1 and 3 launch from ID/EX ALU op[3], and seed 2
launches from op[4]. These paths end at EX/MEM alu_result bits 27, 6,
and 3 respectively, through execute result-selection logic. The reports
are under .tmp/hyp-20260905-003-r1s2-validation/cores/bench/generated/
pnr_seed{1,2,3}/nextpnr.log; synth.json maps the named flops to these bits.
Predecoding the ALU operation before its pipeline register targets the
measured launch path without changing instruction latency.

The bench log's previous micro_opt, hyp-20260905-001-r1s0, changed
register-file read selection and gained only 0.54% with identical cycle
counts. There is no prior registered ALU-predecode attempt in this log.
LESSONS.md records the successful target predictor and the limited cycle
benefit of the pending-store attempt. This proposal preserves the current
predictor and concentrates on execute control timing.

title: Split execution into a fast ALU and an eight-cycle divider
motivation:
The bench ALU places combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU hardware behind the
same forwarded operands and result selection as ordinary integer work.
Sharing a bounded iterative execution resource for these four operations
can reduce arithmetic depth, LUT use, and routing pressure without adding
stages to RV32I instructions or multiplication. The current winner scores
319.45 iter/s at 134.68 MHz and uses 10645 LUT4s. Divider removal is a
plausible timing opportunity, not a confirmed current critical path.

LESSONS.md and the bench structural attempt hyp-20260905-002-r1s1 show
only 0.75% fewer CoreMark cycles from store buffering; most of that
candidate's fitness gain came from Fmax. The adopted target predictor
already reduces control-transfer bubbles. A dedicated multicycle divide
execution path therefore offers a more substantial new structural bet.

Read-only reference hyp-20260428-010-r6s0 in cores/v1 successfully removed
combinational division, reporting 159.92 MHz and 5888 LUT4s on that
different core. Its 32-step hardware divider used shorter ALTOPS timing,
so its formal result does not establish this proposal's control timing.
An earlier reference attempt failed selftest cosim, making operand capture
and exactly-once completion essential. Bench has no recorded divider-split
attempt. Low timed-region DIV/REM traffic is an expectation to verify,
rather than a reason to omit those instructions or arithmetic checks.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Partition execution into the existing one-cycle integer/multiply datapath
and one blocking, eight-cycle divide/remainder engine. Only legal valid
DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU instructions enter the engine. Retain the current
pipeline depth and forwarding for every other instruction, including all
four multiply variants. This changes execution-resource scheduling and
pipeline advancement; it does not add another retirement channel.

Implement unsigned restoring division with four quotient bits computed
per clock, using four cascaded shift/subtract/select steps and one shared
remainder/quotient state. Perform the first four steps on the accepting
launch edge and the remaining seven groups on the next seven edges.
Normalize signed operands on launch and include quotient/remainder sign
correction in the final result capture. Do not add separate normalization
or correction cycles. Capture the original operands and operation at
launch; changing live forwarding values afterward cannot affect the
operation. Preserve truncation toward zero, remainder sign matching the
dividend, quotient all-ones on division by zero, original dividend on
remainder by zero, and INT_MIN/-1 quotient INT_MIN with remainder zero.
Special cases use the same eight-edge schedule. No real / or % operator
remains in the synthesized execution datapath.

Use request acceptance and a retained result-valid/result-ready handshake.
Launch once when a valid legal divide is in ID/EX, the engine is idle,
and an older EX/MEM memory instruction is not blocking advancement.
Freeze the fetch PC and ID/EX while the divide is incomplete. Retain PC,
instruction, destination, control, and exact predicted_next_pc in ID/EX;
latch both post-forwarded source values separately for arithmetic and
RVFI, since older WB values can disappear while the divider runs.

Separate the divider wait from the existing data-memory hold. While
dividing, let older EX/MEM and MEM/WB instructions drain once, then put
complete bubbles into EX/MEM, clearing valid and all write/memory control
bits. Merely holding the previous EX/MEM instruction or clearing valid
alone is insufficient because existing bus/forwarding logic also reads
its control fields. A real data-bus stall still holds EX/MEM and retains
MEM/WB forwarding payload with valid cleared, exactly as today. Starting
or accepting a divide result must never override that older memory hold.

Once the result is valid and EX/MEM can accept it, advance the divide
exactly once with its saved operands and original instruction metadata,
and release ID/EX to the next instruction. Hold result-valid and data
until that acceptance; never relaunch the held instruction or publish a
partial quotient. Forward the completed result through the existing
EX/MEM and MEM/WB routes, including immediate dependent arithmetic,
loads, stores, branches, JALR, and another divide. No younger instruction
overtakes the divide or issues a memory request before it completes.

Qualify EX resolution, predictor training, and mismatch recovery by actual
instruction advancement, including divide completion. A stale prediction
on a divide still recovers to its architectural PC+4 exactly once. Keep
the current predictor organization and all ordinary branch behavior.
Reset cancels the pending operation and prevents a stale completion.

Preserve all eight existing ALTOPS formulas. For DIV/REM, capture the
corresponding existing formula result from the accepted operands and
release it using the SAME eight-cycle controller, holds, and completion
handshake as real arithmetic. Do not use a shorter formal-only schedule,
bypass the engine in formal, or change formal depths. With the first
digit group on launch and correction on the last group, ready-bus
execution must satisfy the existing ten-cycle successor-retirement
window, including a divide following redirect recovery; verify this in
the unchanged liveness gate. This timing bound is a design requirement.

Expect approximately 12% higher fitness from reduced divider hardware
and timing pressure, with medium confidence. Four subtract steps plus
launch normalization or final correction may still limit Fmax, and any
timed DIV/REM instructions add cycles. Measure both effects using the
unchanged bracketed, stalled CoreMark evaluation and median of three
FPGA seeds against 319.45; report LUT/FF use and inspect the resulting
critical path. This estimate is not a measured result. Preserve nret=1,
every external port and RVFI field, strict retirement order, decoder and
trap rules, memory ordering and bounds, marker handshakes, canonical
CoreMark CRC/UART validation, and every existing correctness check.

implementation_notes:
# Eight-edge divider implementation

Implemented the proposed divider split in `cores/bench` only. The requested implementation notes are at the worktree root, as specified in instruction 5; all RTL and test changes are confined to the permitted bench files.

## Implementation

- Added `rtl/div_unit.sv`: one restoring remainder/quotient state, four cascaded shift/subtract/select steps per edge, first group on request acceptance, and corrected registered result on edge eight. Signed normalization happens on launch. Divide by zero, signed overflow, and remainder signs use the same schedule as ordinary operands.
- Integrated the engine into `alu.sv` with request-ready and retained result-valid/result-ready signals. Ordinary integer operations and all four multiplies remain combinational. All eight original ALTOPS formulas are preserved; DIV/REM capture their formula from accepted operands and use the identical eight-edge controller.
- EX saves both post-forwarded source operands for RVFI while ID/EX retains the instruction, PC, exact prediction, destination, and controls. Request readiness prevents relaunch while computing or retaining a result. The result advances once through the existing EX/MEM and MEM/WB path.
- Added a separate divide interlock to EX, hazard control, and core wiring. Divide waits freeze fetch and ID/EX but drain older instructions once and insert complete EX/MEM bubbles. Actual memory holds retain their original EX/MEM priority and MEM/WB forwarding behavior. Resolution, predictor training, and redirects occur only when EX advances, including divide completion.
- Reset cancels computation and retained results. The nret=1 top-level ports, retirement logic, decoder/traps, predictor organization, register file, forwarding unit, and memory stage remain unchanged.
- Expanded integrated ALU tests and pipeline tests. No gate, formal depth, arithmetic expectation, or existing assertion was weakened.

The controller produces result-valid after edge eight; EX/MEM accepts on edge nine and MEM/WB retires on edge ten. A divide after a cold redirect retires exactly ten cycles after the redirecting instruction. Back-to-back divides retire nine cycles apart with ready buses.

## Local validation

- Required Verilator lint command: PASS, no warnings. Also PASS with `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` defined.
- Yosys elaboration/process/optimization followed by `select -assert-none` for `$div`, `$mod`, `$divfloor`, and `$modfloor`: PASS. No real division/remainder operator remains in the synthesized execution datapath.
- Complete cocotb suite: PASS, all seven pytest runner cases. ALU runs in real and ALTOPS builds, each checking 185 boundary/deterministic vectors per M operation plus existing exact tests. Tests cover eight-edge completion, changing live operands/opcodes, rejected requests while occupied, retained results, ready asserted before completion, fast ALU operation during division, reset at every phase, and consecutive requests.
- Pipeline tests: PASS. Coverage includes EX/MEM and MEM/WB operands, stalled load dependencies, retained older WB payload, consecutive divides, rd=x0, 34 vector pairs for every DIV/REM variant, immediate and one-gap consumers, all four multiply consumers, loads, store data/address, branches, JALR, redirect recovery, stale predictions, simultaneous bus stalls, memory markers, illegal/flushed instructions, and reset during execution. Assertions check saved RVFI operands, full bubbles, strict order/PC chaining, exactly-once launch/completion/resolution, writes and memory requests, and ready-bus retirement bounds.
- Unchanged `bash formal/run_all.sh`, selecting bench nret=1: **PASS, 53 passed / 0 failed**, including `liveness_ch0`, `unique_ch0`, and all four DIV/REM instruction checks. First completed formal suite passed; zero RTL fix retries. Formal ran in a scratch copy under `$TMPDIR`, with unchanged wrapper, checks, and depth settings.
- Unchanged selftest cosim plus CoreMark CRC gate: PASS, two ELFs tested. Additional selftest cosim with both random bus stalls and seeds 3735928559, 1, and 42: PASS, 115 retirements each, byte-exact against the unchanged ISS.
- Full real-arithmetic `formal-deep` was not run. ALTOPS formal validates the real controller latency and routing, while real arithmetic is checked by the simulation vectors and cosim.

## Measured FPGA and benchmark results

The unchanged local evaluator reports:

| Metric | Prior winner | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Median Fmax | 134.68 MHz | 135.03 MHz |
| Fitness | 319.45 iter/s | 320.28 iter/s |
| LUT4 | 10,645 | 5,871 |
| FF | 2,075 | 2,292 |
| Bracketed stalled CoreMark cycles | 4,215,937 | 4,215,937 |

All three FPGA seeds routed successfully: seed 1 = 135.03 MHz, seed 2 = 144.68 MHz, seed 3 = 126.39 MHz. Fitness improved **0.26%**, LUT4 use fell **44.85%**, and FF use rose **10.46%**. The approximately 12% anticipated fitness gain was not realized.

The baseline cycle count was independently reproduced from the original HEAD bench RTL using the same ELF and unchanged stalled harness. A streamed full candidate retirement trace contained 2,937,037 instructions: the measured region executed 93,960 MULs and **zero DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU instructions**. The complete program executed two DIVUs outside the markers. Thus divider latency did not affect the scored cycle count.

All three post-route critical paths run through predictor tag lookup and counter write control. For the median seed, the path starts at `cpu.u_if.tag_q.0.1_RAD_DFFR_Q_3.Q` and ends at `cpu.u_if.counter_q.1.0.WRE`: 7.41 ns total, comprising 3.77 ns logic and 3.63 ns routing. The divider is not on the reported critical path. The small fitness change and substantial seed spread do not establish the predicted timing benefit.

## Benchmark contract discrepancy and supplemental 6 KB run

The request describes a 6 KB performance workload with CRCs d4b0/be52/5e47. The checked-in `bench/programs/Makefile` actually defaults to `COREMARK_SIZE=2000`, and the unchanged evaluator requires the 2 KB CRC set e714/1fd7/8e3a (seed e9f5, final fcaf). The 319.45 reference is consistent with this checked-in configuration. No benchmark source, Makefile, evaluator, or CRC check was changed; the primary fitness above uses the unchanged evaluation.

A supplemental scratch build used the existing `COREMARK_SIZE=6000` option, `-O3`, and ITERATIONS=10 with both random stalls. It passed EBREAK, memory bounds, marker bracketing, the literal `Correct operation validated.`, and exact CRCs: seed 8a02, list d4b0, matrix be52, state 5e47, final 5949. It measured 30,823,120 bracketed cycles, equivalent to 43.81 iter/s at the measured 135.03 MHz median. This supplemental score is not compared to the differently configured 319.45 baseline.

## Evidence and remaining concerns

Scratch artifacts are under `$TMPDIR/hyp-20260905-002-r2s1-checks`; post-route reports are in its `cores/bench/generated/pnr_seed{1,2,3}/nextpnr.log`. Logs alongside that scratch directory use the prefix `hyp-20260905-002-r2s1-`, including `formal.log`, `unit-tests.log`, `cosim.log`, `selftest-stalls.log`, `fpga.log`, `baseline-cycles.log`, `div-traffic.log`, and `6k.log`.

No functional deviation from the proposed divider schedule was needed. The material limitations are the unchanged predictor critical path, the small measured fitness gain relative to seed variation, and the workload-dependent eight extra EX hold cycles for each divide/remainder compared with the old combinational ALU. Synthesis emitted only the expected array-to-wire lowering messages for the four combinational digit steps; required lint is clean.
lesson: - 2026-09-05 hyp-20260905-002-r2s1 (improvement, +0.26%): An eight-cycle DIV/REM engine cut LUT4 use 44.85% without changing CoreMark cycles because the timed region executes no DIV/REM, but predictor tag lookup and counter-write control remained the critical path, leaving the fitness gain small relative to FPGA seed variation.

title: Two-way target prediction at unchanged 16-entry capacity
motivation:
The predictor in hyp-20260905-003-r1s2 cut stalled CoreMark cycles by
6.14% and reached 319.45 fitness, establishing that removing the
combinational frontend's one-slot recovery bubbles is valuable. Its
16-entry direct-mapped table indexes PC[5:2], so recurring branches and
jumps separated by multiples of 64 bytes evict each other's targets
and two-bit direction history. Such interference can persist even when
only two control-flow PCs are hot. The experiment log contains one
predictor attempt and no associativity experiment; conflict frequency
has not yet been measured. Since the winning predictor already added
about 11% LUT/FF usage, retaining its entry count makes associativity a
focused way to seek further cycle savings with limited storage growth.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Reorganize the existing target predictor into eight sets with two ways
per set, retaining sixteen total entries. Index both fetch and EX
resolution with PC[4:2]. Each way stores valid, the full PC[31:5] tag,
aligned target[31:2], and the existing two-bit saturating counter. Add
one replacement bit per set, naming the next victim when both ways are
valid. Total logical table state becomes 968 bits: sixteen 60-bit
entries plus eight replacement bits, versus the current 944 bits.
Use separate way arrays so two eight-entry reads and tag comparisons
operate in parallel. Combine the matching taken way's target into the
existing predicted_next_pc selection; otherwise select PC+4. Keep the
lookup combinational and dependent only on registered predictor state
and fetch PC. There is no additional pipeline stage or EX-update bypass.

On each existing resolve_valid pulse, compute both full-tag matches
from the resolving PC. For a legal taken branch or legal jump, update
the matching way. On a miss, select invalid way 0 first, then invalid
way 1, then the set's recorded victim. Write the tag and aligned target.
A new conditional branch starts at 2'b10; a matching taken branch
increments its own counter with saturation; a jump sets 2'b11. A legal
not-taken branch decrements only its matching counter, retaining the
target, and does not allocate on a miss. After any legal control-flow
hit, including not-taken and saturated-counter hits, or any allocation,
name the other way as the next victim. Replacement state changes only
on these EX events, so wrong-path fetches cannot affect replacement.
An illegal, trapping, or non-control resolution invalidates only a
matching way and leaves the other tag's entry intact. Always update a
hit before considering allocation, ensuring that a PC cannot occupy
both ways. Reset all valid and replacement bits; payloads remain
unreset and are masked by validity.

Preserve the current exact predicted_next_pc capture through ID/EX,
architectural next-PC comparison for every advancing EX instruction,
and RVFI reporting of the resolved destination. Training remains
qualified by in.valid && !stall && !reset. Prediction consumption,
recovery priority over instruction-bus backpressure, data-stall holds,
trap handling, and the external nret=1 interface retain their existing
behavior. All instruction and target addresses retain their full
architectural width; the indexing policy is independent of workload.

The expected benefit is fewer repeated conflict misses and less loss
of branch hysteresis. Alternating control transfers at two PCs sharing
the old index should both remain warm and avoid recovery bubbles.

title: Localize predictor training to remove indexed feedback muxes
motivation:
The current winner reaches 320.28 iter/s at 135.03 MHz. Its implementation
notes report predictor tag lookup to counter write control as the critical
path in all three routed seeds; the median path is 7.41 ns, with 3.77 ns
logic and 3.63 ns routing. In if_stage.sv, training reads a dynamically
indexed tag and counter, computes one shared resolve_hit and counter
update, then distributes the result back to the selected entry.

Previous micro_opt attempts changed register-file reads (+0.54% fitness)
and registered ALU selects (-3.92%), without reducing CoreMark cycles.
The divider split left the predictor bottleneck intact, while two-way
prediction lost timing with essentially unchanged cycles. A local rewrite
of the existing training feedback path directly targets the reported
bottleneck without changing prediction policy.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace only the predictor's shared, dynamically indexed training logic
with sixteen constant-index entry update blocks in rtl/if_stage.sv.
For entry i, decode selected_i = resolve_valid && (resolve_pc[5:2] == i)
and independently compute hit_i = valid_q[i] &&
(tag_q[i] == resolve_pc[31:6]). Read that entry's tag and two counter bits
through constant indices, so tag comparison and counter next-state
calculation operate locally in parallel with index decoding. Do not
reduce hits into a shared resolve_hit or select an old counter through
a resolve-index mux before calculating its update. Each state bit must
have one sequential owner, with reset taking precedence.

Preserve the exact existing transition rules. Only the selected entry
may change. An illegal, trapping, or non-control resolution clears valid
only on a local full-tag hit. A legal jump writes valid, tag and target
and sets its counter to 11. A legal taken branch writes valid, tag and
target, initializes a miss to 10, and saturating-increments a hit. A
legal not-taken branch saturating-decrements only a matching entry,
retains its target, and does nothing on a miss. Encode increment and
decrement as local two-bit Boolean equations or complete transition
cases, including self-transitions at 11 and 00; avoid a shared arithmetic
result and separate saturation qualification of a shared write enable.
Reset clears all valid bits while leaving payloads unreset as today.

Keep the sixteen-entry direct-mapped organization, PC[5:2] index, full
PC[31:6] tags, aligned 30-bit targets, two-bit hysteresis, and existing
combinational fetch lookup. Training remains visible only after its
clock edge, with no update bypass or additional register stage. Preserve
resolve_valid qualification from EX, exact predicted_next_pc capture,
recovery priority, stall behavior, and all nret=1 bus and RVFI semantics.
This is one implementation-level timing optimization of predictor
training; instruction scheduling and prediction decisions remain equal
cycle by cycle for the same inputs.

Removing the resolve-side read-mux, shared compare/update, and writeback
distribution chain should raise median Fmax with unchanged bracketed
cycles. Estimate a five percent fitness gain, approximately 336.29 iter/s
at 141.78 MHz under the current scored configuration. This is a hypothesis,
not a measurement. Replicated tag comparisons, increased resolve-signal
fanout, or losing LUTRAM packing can increase area and routing delay;
the unchanged fetch/recovery path may also become limiting.

Validate public prediction behavior against the existing policy across
all indices and colliding full tags, then run the unchanged unit, formal,
stalled cosim and FPGA gates. Compare against 320.28 using the same ELF,
ready schedule and benchmark configuration, full-precision iterations
divided by bracketed cycles, and three-seed median Fmax. Report LUT/FF
usage and the new critical path. Require identical scored cycle counts
and preserve all CRC, UART validation, memory-bound and timing-marker
checks. Prior notes distinguish the scored workload from a supplemental

title: Pipeline resolution feedback with registered predictor-row reads
motivation:
The current bench winner reaches 320.28 iter/s at 135.03 MHz. Its
hyp-20260905-002-r2s1 implementation notes identify the predictor's
indexed tag lookup through counter-write control as the critical path
in all three FPGA seeds; the median path is 7.41 ns. Removing nearly
half the LUTs with a separate divider improved fitness only 0.26%,
with unchanged CoreMark cycles. The other prior structural attempt,
hyp-20260905-002-r1s1, saved only 0.75% of cycles by buffering stores.
These results favor splitting the measured feedback path over another
backend resource change. LESSONS.md also records the timing regression
from two-way prediction, despite essentially unchanged CoreMark cycles.

In the present if_stage.sv, one cycle contains an indexed table read,
a full-tag comparison, saturating-counter decisions, and table write
control. Registering the selected row before comparison creates a
structural pipeline boundary in this read/modify/write transaction.
The prediction algorithm, capacity, instruction pipeline, and immediate
EX recovery can retain their existing organization.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split resolved-instruction feedback into a row-read stage and an update
stage inside if_stage. Retain exactly sixteen direct-mapped entries,
PC[5:2] indexing, full PC[31:6] tags, aligned 30-bit targets, and the
existing two-bit counter policy. The single architectural change is
adding one register boundary to the training transaction; do not add
an instruction pipeline stage or change execution-resource scheduling.

On edge N with resolve_valid asserted, capture the resolution's index,
PC tag, target, legal/branch/jump/taken flags, and the selected row's
valid, tag, and two-bit counter into a maintenance register. Capture
raw row state here, not an already-computed tag hit or counter update:
the indexed read must end at this register. The existing target need
not be read for training because neither hit detection nor counter
arithmetic consumes it. Carry a separate maintenance-valid bit.

During the following cycle, compare the captured tags and compute the
row update solely from the captured event and row state. Commit it on
edge N+1. A legal jump writes its full target and counter 11. A legal
taken branch writes its target, allocates counter 10 on a miss, and
increments with saturation on a hit. A legal not-taken branch only
decrements a matching counter with saturation, retaining the target
and allocating nothing on a miss. An illegal, trapping, or non-control
resolution invalidates only a matching tag. Preserve the existing
field-specific write enables and full architectural address widths.
In particular, no live indexed tag lookup may feed the update-stage
write enable, or the proposed timing cut would disappear.

Sustain one resolution per cycle by committing the older transaction
while accepting the next. Handle their read-after-write hazard with
explicit maintenance forwarding: when the committing transaction and
incoming resolution address the same index, capture the older
transaction's post-update valid/tag/counter as the incoming row
snapshot instead of the pre-edge table values. Forward the complete
logical state of those fields, including invalidation, allocation,
saturation, and unchanged fields. Compare indices for this bypass,
not tags: different PCs aliasing one row require forwarding too.
This bypass is confined to the maintenance pipeline. After draining,
table state must equal applying the accepted resolution stream in
order under the original update policy; no event may be lost or
counted twice, including consecutive updates to the same branch.

Set maintenance-valid from resolve_valid every non-reset edge, rather
than holding it on a frontend or backend stall. A previously accepted
event commits once even if IF is stalled, a later divide is waiting,
or a younger instruction redirects. Acceptance still uses the existing
advancing-EX resolve_valid qualification; held EX instructions cannot
enqueue repeatedly. Reset has priority over both capture and commit,
clears all table valid bits and maintenance-valid, and cannot permit
a pre-reset transaction to repopulate the predictor afterward.

Fetch continues to consult committed table state only. There is no
pending-update bypass to predicted_next_pc, no training backpressure,
and no extra delay on the EX actual-next-PC comparison or redirect.
Preserve the exact prediction accepted with each instruction through
ID/EX and retain resolved architectural pc_next at RVFI retirement.
Recovery still overrides imem stalls, and dmem/divide holds keep their
current priorities. Training becomes visible one cycle later than
today; a very short cold loop can therefore mispredict an additional
time. Warm self-jumps must still sustain one retirement per cycle,
and each recovery retains its existing single younger-slot bubble.

Expect a 6% fitness improvement, with medium confidence, from separating
the table-read mux from tag comparison and update write control. This
is an estimate, not a measured result. The maintenance bypass could
become critical, delayed training can increase cycles, and fetch or
EX recovery may set the new timing limit. Evaluate the unchanged
marker-bracketed stalled CoreMark workload and three-seed median Fmax;
report exact iterations/cycles, LUT/FF usage, and post-route critical
paths. Compare the fitness product with 320.28 using the same workload
configuration, identifying the configuration in the results. Preserve
nret=1 and every external port, all RVFI order/operand/trap rules,
decoder legality, divider and ALTOPS behavior, memory handshakes and
bounds, and the required CoreMark CRC/UART/marker checks. All formal
configurations, test harnesses, and evaluation gates remain intact.

implementation_notes:
# Registered predictor maintenance: hyp-20260905-002-r3s1

Implemented the proposed training pipeline. All local evaluation gates pass.
The unchanged gate reports **340.22 iter/s**, with **143.41 MHz** three-seed
median Fmax, **5,920 LUT4s**, and **2,382 FFs**. Using the unrounded fitness
product, the improvement over the supplied 320.28 is **6.2245848777%**.

## Implementation

- Only `cores/bench/rtl/if_stage.sv` changes hardware. At edge N it captures
  the resolution index, full 26-bit tag, aligned 30-bit target, four event
  flags, and raw selected-row valid/tag/counter. It does not capture a hit
  result, a computed counter, or the old target.
- Captured tags and counter drive the following cycle's update. Edge N+1
  commits it while capturing the next event. Update write enables have no
  live indexed tag/counter input. Valid, tag/target, and counter writes
  retain the original field-specific policy, including saturated no-ops.
- Same-index maintenance forwarding captures the committing transaction's
  complete post-update valid/tag/counter, including unchanged fields,
  invalidation, and replacement by another full tag. This bypass never
  reaches fetch prediction.
- Maintenance-valid is assigned from resolve-valid on every non-reset edge.
  IF/backend holds and younger redirects do not hold or cancel accepted
  training. Reset cancels capture and commit, clears maintenance-valid and
  all table valids, and leaves unused payloads unreset.
- Capacity, indexing, tag/target widths, prediction algorithm, EX resolution
  qualification and immediate recovery, instruction-stage count, execution
  scheduling, nret=1, external ports, RVFI, decoder, divider, and ALTOPS are
  unchanged. No architectural deviation from the hypothesis.

## Tests

- `test_if_stage.py`: independent sequential policy model checked before
  and after edges, exact committed table fields and captured raw snapshots,
  one event per edge, counter saturation/thresholds, target retention,
  different-tag same-index replacement, invalidation/allocation, misses,
  no-ops, different indices, idle drain, full addresses, no fetch bypass,
  and reset cancellation. A deterministic 1,200-cycle random stream includes
  aliases, bubbles, stalls, redirects, and resets, followed by a full probe.
- `test_pipeline.py`: applies the model to every existing pipeline test and
  checks redirects against the prediction actually accepted with the
  instruction. Adds short branch loops and pending-update drain during
  imem stalls, dmem holds, divide waits, overlapping redirects, and reset.
  Existing JALR target changes, stale code/traps, held-EX exactly-once
  checks, operand/order/PC-chain checks, wrong-path stores, memory, and
  arithmetic assertions remain active.
- Intentional latency expectation changes: self-jumps have two cold misses,
  each followed by one younger-slot bubble; warm retirement remains one
  per cycle. Alternating full-tag aliases can hit an older committed row
  before its pending replacement commits, so that test now asserts the
  exact delayed-update prediction/redirect sequence instead of all misses.

## Local validation

- Required `verilator --lint-only -Wall -Wno-MULTITOP -sv
  +incdir+cores/bench/rtl cores/bench/rtl/*.sv`: PASS, no warnings/errors.
- Full cocotb suite: **7 pytest runners passed**, including **38 pipeline
  tests**, **4 IF tests**, and both real-arithmetic and ALTOPS ALU builds.
- Local formal status: **PASS, 53 passed / 0 failed**, using the unchanged
  `bash formal/run_all.sh`, `RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl`, `CORE_NAME=bench`,
  `JOBS=6`; automatic nret=1 selection chose `wrapper_si.sv` and
  `checks_si.cfg`. The first shell invocation exited before generation
  because its Python lacked PyYAML; selecting the installed conda Python
  resolved this. First actual proof run passed; no counterexample and no
  RTL fix/retry for formal. Formal-deep was not run; arithmetic is unchanged.
- Unchanged cosim evaluator: **PASS, 2 ELFs** (selftest full RVFI comparison
  and stalled CoreMark CRC/UART validation).
- Unchanged `make fpga TARGET=bench`, with `NRET=1` and
  `BENCH=fpga/core_bench_si.sv`: PASS, all three seeds routed and benchmark
  validation completed. `git diff --check`: PASS.
- Formal, cosim, and FPGA run in an isolated `$TMPDIR` copy; 48 evaluated
  RTL/config/harness/source files were byte-compared with the worktree.
  No protected harness, source, configuration, or other core was edited.

## Workload configuration and exact performance

The checked-in `bench/programs/Makefile` defaults to `TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=2000`,
`-O3`, and the evaluator's CRC goldens are for that 2 KB configuration.
This conflicts with the prompt's 6 KB description. The gates were preserved.
Both sizes were measured separately using the unchanged harness,
`ITERATIONS=10`, `--bench --istall --dstall`, default stall seed
`0xDEADBEEF`, and only the `0x10000100` start / `0x10000104` stop bracket.
The original HEAD RTL was rebuilt in scratch to measure baseline cycles.
Baseline Fmax and resource counts below are the supplied winner's values;
baseline FPGA routing was not repeated.

| Configuration | Original RTL cycles | New RTL cycles | Original iter/s at 135.03 MHz | New iter/s at 143.41 MHz |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Unchanged gate: 2 KB, -O3, 10 iterations, both stalls | 4,215,937 | 4,215,262 | 320.2846721856 | 340.2161004464 |
| Supplemental: 6 KB, -O3, 10 iterations, both stalls | 30,823,120 | 30,822,790 | 43.8080246257 | 46.5272611597 |

The 2 KB baseline reproduces **320.28** under the same configuration.
The new exact throughput is `10 / 4215262 = 2.372331779139707e-6`
iterations/cycle; fitness is `143410000 * 10 / 4215262`.
It saves 675 bracketed cycles. The 6 KB result saves 330 cycles and improves
the same-configuration fitness by **6.2071653704%**; comparing its absolute
score directly with 320.28 would mix workloads.

The primary gate validates its unchanged 2 KB goldens: seedcrc=e9f5,
crclist=e714, crcmatrix=1fd7, crcstate=8e3a, crcfinal=fcaf.
The supplemental 6 KB run explicitly checked the requested crclist=d4b0,
crcmatrix=be52, crcstate=5e47, plus seedcrc=8a02 and crcfinal=5949.
Both baseline and candidate supplemental runs reached EBREAK, had
`oob=false`, reported 10 iterations and the literal
`Correct operation validated.`, and contained valid timing markers.
For new 6 KB RTL, start=53,747 and stop=30,876,537. The old stop was
30,876,867 with the same start. The UART's compiler-flags string remains
the inherited hardcoded `-O2 -march=rv32im`; the actual build command is
`-O3`. The UART size field is per algorithm (666 for 2 KB, 2000 for 6 KB).

## Three-seed post-route timing

Device: `GW2A-LV18QN88C8/I7`, family `GW2A-18C`, unchanged Tang Nano 20K
constraints. These are final post-route reports, not placement estimates.

| Seed | Fmax MHz | Critical path ns | Logic ns | Routing ns |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 143.41 | 6.97 | 3.95 | 3.02 |
| 2 | 137.51 | 7.27 | 2.32 | 4.95 |
| 3 | 155.74 | 6.42 | 2.32 | 4.10 |

- Seed 1: `cpu.u_id.reg_q_DFFRE_Q_175.Q` (`cpu.id_ex_w[54]`) through
  hazard/control logic to `cpu.u_ex.reg_q_DFFR_Q_63.D`.
- Seed 2: `cpu.u_id.reg_q_DFFRE_Q_161.Q` (`cpu.id_ex_w[11]`) through
  hazard/divide-wait control to `cpu.u_id.reg_q_DFFRE_Q_71.RESET`.
- Seed 3: same source and hazard/divide-wait control class as seed 2,
  ending at `cpu.u_id.reg_q_DFFRE_Q_98.RESET`.

Median Fmax increases from 135.03 to 143.41 MHz. The median critical path
falls from the supplied 7.41 ns to 6.97 ns. None of the three final
critical paths crosses the predictor indexed maintenance lookup.
All seeds use 5,920 LUT4s and 2,382 DFFs, versus 5,871 / 2,292 supplied
for the winner: **+49 LUTs, +90 FFs**. The maintenance payload contains
94 source-level bits before synthesis optimization.

## Concerns and evidence

The intended extra cold self-loop miss remains a performance cost, and
alias timing changes can help or hurt particular streams. Observed cycle
changes also include the deterministic stall generator's changed phase.
Maintenance forwarding is combinational but was not the reported timing
limit in any seed. Hazard/control routing is the new measured limit;
this change intentionally does not alter it.

Scratch evidence directory:
`$TMPDIR/hyp-r3-validation-3dg8_bd1/`

It contains `formal-gate.log`, `cocotb-gate.log`,
`cosim-gate-result.log`, `fpga-gate.log`, `comparison.json`, the raw
`baseline-2k.jsonl`, `baseline-6k.jsonl`, `candidate-6k.jsonl`, and
`cores/bench/generated/pnr_seed{1,2,3}/nextpnr.log` with the complete
post-route paths. Implementation notes are at the worktree root as
requested by instruction 5 and consumed by the orchestrator's notes reader.
lesson: - 2026-09-05 hyp-20260905-002-r3s1 (regression, +6.23%): Registering raw predictor-row reads before tag comparison/counter writes, with same-index post-update forwarding for back-to-back resolutions, removed the maintenance lookup from all three critical paths and raised median Fmax from 135.03 to 143.41 MHz with essentially unchanged stalled CoreMark cycles, exposing hazard/divide-wait control as the next timing limit.

title: Row-local predictor metadata training to remove the indexed feedback path
motivation:
The existing 16-entry direct-mapped predictor already reduced stalled
CoreMark cycles by 6.14%. The two-way experiment hyp-20260905-003-r2s2
measured 4,220,017 cycles versus 4,215,937 for the direct-mapped winner,
while lowering median Fmax to 124.94 MHz. More lookup complexity has
therefore not paid for itself in this core. The current winner,
hyp-20260905-002-r2s1, reports all three post-route critical paths through
predictor tag lookup and counter-write control. Its median path runs
from tag storage to counter WRE in 7.41 ns, with 3.77 ns logic and
3.63 ns routing. The current RTL reads tag_q[resolve_index] and
counter_q[resolve_index], computes a shared hit/update decision, and
writes back through the same variable index. Removing this training
feedback path is a focused opportunity to raise the current 135.03 MHz

acts on an existing resolve_valid pulse. A legal jump writes its tag

Legal jumps train strongly taken; taken branches allocate weakly taken or saturating-increment a hit; not-taken branches decrement only a hit and preserve targets; non-control and illegal/trapping resolutions invalidate only a matching tag. hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure only the resolve-side full-tag equality in each existing
metadata row of rtl/if_stage.sv. Replace the unconstrained 26-bit
comparison with an explicit balanced tree suited to four-input LUTs.
First compute thirteen independent two-bit equalities: pair_eq[g]
compares tag_q[2*g +: 2] with resolve_pc[6 + 2*g +: 2], for g=0..12.
Each equality has exactly four variable inputs. Next form four
parallel reductions over pair_eq[3:0], [6:4], [9:7], and [12:10].
AND those four results to obtain full_tag_equal, then qualify it with
the row's valid_q to obtain the existing row_hit. All 26 tag bits
participate; no shortened tag, hash, or approximate match is allowed.

Preserve these local pair and group boundaries with source-level
Yosys keep attributes on their combinational wires, so the mapper
cannot simply absorb the whole expression back into the current
serial update cone. Use portable combinational SystemVerilog in all
simulation, formal, and synthesis builds. The intended equality
network has three LUT4 levels before validity/update qualification.
Confirm the boundaries survive the unchanged synthesis flow by
inspecting the mapped netlist; an equivalent source expression alone
does not demonstrate the intended timing optimization. Keep reset,
resolve_valid, row selection, and event qualification outside the
equality tree. No register, enable, or maintenance stage is added.

Retain the sixteen scalar valid/tag/counter rows, their current
field-specific update rules, counter encoding and saturation, and
the separate indexed 16x30 target array. Fetch still uses the current
indexed full-tag lookup. A legal jump allocates strongly taken; a
taken branch allocates weakly taken or increments a hit; a not-taken
branch decrements only a hit and retains the target; a non-control
or illegal/trapping resolution invalidates only a matching row.
Invalid payloads remain masked, reset clears valid bits with priority,
and unselected rows retain state. Training still becomes visible
after the same edge, with no update bypass. Predictions, redirects,
and accepted instructions must agree cycle by cycle with the current
RTL for identical input schedules, including same-row collisions.

This is one logic-mapping micro-optimization. It leaves pipeline
scheduling, predictor policy and capacity, instruction latency,
arithmetic and ALTOPS, decoder legality, memory handshakes, RVFI,
nret=1, and every top-level port unchanged. The estimated fitness
gain is five percent through Fmax alone, with unchanged bracketed
cycles. Confidence is medium: preserving reduction boundaries can
increase LUT use or routing, resolve-PC fanout remains, and another
control path may become limiting. This estimate is not a measurement.

title: Pipeline row-addressed resolution events before local predictor updates
motivation:
The current bench winner scores 350.46 iter/s at 147.75 MHz. Its
hyp-20260905-003-r3s2 implementation notes identify all three critical
paths as ID/EX resolve-PC registers through local predictor tag matching
to metadata enables; the median path is 6.77 ns, including 3.72 ns of
routing. Row-local metadata removed the indexed feedback mux, but live
EX PC bits still feed sixteen full-tag comparisons and tag-write paths.

The structural history favors a targeted timing cut. Store buffering
in hyp-20260905-002-r1s1 saved only 0.75% of CoreMark cycles; separating
division in hyp-20260905-002-r2s1 substantially reduced area but improved
fitness only 0.26%. The registered row-read experiment
hyp-20260905-002-r3s1 reached 143.41 MHz with nearly unchanged cycles,
losing to the current winner. It captured selected metadata and needed
forwarding between maintenance transactions. The current local rows
permit a different cut: register each resolution at its destination row
before comparison, then update that row directly from its current state.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one pipeline boundary to resolution maintenance, using a private
pending-event register at each of the sixteen existing metadata rows.
This is one structural retiming of the feedback transaction. Keep the
instruction pipeline, immediate EX redirect, predictor algorithm,
capacity, fetch lookup, and execution-resource scheduling unchanged.

Each row gets a pending-valid bit, full 26-bit resolving PC tag, and
two-bit command. Encode the four commands as matching-tag invalidation
for illegal/trapping/non-control instructions, legal jump, legal taken
branch, and legal not-taken branch. Classification uses the existing
resolve_legal/branch/jump/taken outputs, with illegality taking priority.
On edge N, pending_valid[row] becomes resolve_valid &&
(resolve_pc[5:2] == row). Update that row's pending tag and command only
on this acceptance; otherwise retain its payload. These independently
enabled registers must remain local to their rows, rather than becoming
one shared registered PC broadcast into sixteen comparisons. Capture
the event only; do not read, snapshot, or compare old table metadata
on this edge. At most one row accepts per cycle, without backpressure.

On edge N+1, each row with its old pending-valid asserted commits using
its private pending tag/command and its current local valid/tag/counter.
A jump writes the pending tag, sets valid, and sets the counter to 11.
A taken branch writes the tag and valid, allocates counter 10 on a miss,
or increments a hit with saturation. A not-taken branch decrements only
a matching counter with saturation and retains its target. Invalidation
clears only a matching row's valid bit. Preserve all other fields.
Commit-time tag comparisons, saturation, tag data, and metadata enables
must have no combinational dependency on live EX resolution inputs.

Commit the old event while accepting the next, including consecutive
events to the same row with different tags. Do not capture a counter or
hit snapshot: the next event sees the preceding event's committed local
state during its own update cycle. Consequently there is no indexed
metadata read and no maintenance forwarding mux. After draining, table
state must equal applying every accepted event in order under the
existing policy, including aliases, invalidations, and saturated updates.

Delay the separate indexed target write by the same edge. Capture one
shared write-valid bit, four-bit index, and full 30-bit aligned target
for a legal jump or taken branch, then write the existing target array
on edge N+1. Its delayed write-valid is refreshed every cycle and is
independent of old tags/counters. Tag, valid, counter, and target changes
for an event become visible together; never publish a new tag with an
old target. Retain the existing indexed target storage implementation.
This adds approximately 499 source-level event-state bits: 16 times
(1+26+2), plus one shared (1+4+30) target-write record.

Refresh pending-valid bits every non-reset edge, even during fetch or
backend stalls. An accepted event commits once while a younger divide
waits, a memory request stalls, or a younger instruction redirects.
Acceptance remains qualified by the existing advancing-EX resolve_valid;
held instructions cannot retrain repeatedly. Reset overrides capture
and commit, clears all pending/table validity, and cancels pending target
writes. Masked payloads need no reset. No added architectural stall is
permitted when a maintenance event is pending.

Fetch consults committed state only, with no pending-event bypass. A
prediction accepted on a commit edge uses pre-edge state. Preserve the
exact predicted next PC carried with each instruction, the EX comparison
against actual next PC for every advancing instruction, and resolved
RVFI next-PC reporting. Training visibility moves one edge later, which
can add cold-loop misses; warm self-jumps must still retire once per
cycle and recovery must still kill only the existing younger slot.
Preserve nret=1 and every external port, ordered retirement, operand
forwarding, decoder and trap rules, real/ALTOPS arithmetic, memory
handshakes and bounds, and every protected evaluation check.

Estimate four percent higher fitness from shorter maintenance paths,
with little change in bracketed cycles. This is unmeasured. Additional
event flops, capture-enable fanout, later training, or the hazard/divide
control path exposed in r3s1 could erase the gain. Inspect the synthesized
cones and three-seed post-route reports: live resolve-PC paths should
terminate at event capture, while tag comparison starts at private row
event registers. Report actual LUT4/FF costs and exact iterations/cycle
times median Fmax, using the same toolchain and workload for comparison.

Run unchanged lint, cocotb, formal, cosim, and FPGA gates. The historical
notes identify the 350.46 score as the existing 2 KB gate and separately
report 30,823,120 cycles for the canonical 6 KB workload. Preserve both
contracts: compare the unchanged scored workload with 350.46, and also
run the required 6 KB, -O3, ten-iteration workload with both bus stalls
against the original RTL. Require canonical d4b0/be52/5e47 CRCs, the
validation literal, bounds checks, and start/stop marker bracketing.
Report the two configurations separately; do not mix their fitnesses
or modify harnesses, benchmark sources, wrappers, or other cores.

implementation_notes:
Implemented the row-addressed resolution-event pipeline in `cores/bench/rtl/if_stage.sv`, with corresponding coverage in `cores/bench/test/test_if_stage.py` and `cores/bench/test/test_pipeline.py`. No other RTL, core configuration, benchmark source, wrapper, harness, or evaluation gate changed. This requested notes file is at the worktree root, as read by the orchestrator and explicitly permitted by its path checks.

Each of the sixteen metadata rows now owns a pending-valid bit, independently enabled 26-bit resolving tag, and two-bit command: invalidate=00, jump=01, taken branch=10, not-taken branch=11. Illegality takes priority. Acceptance captures only the event; it neither reads nor snapshots metadata. Each row commits its old event against its current local valid/tag/counter while accepting the next event, including consecutive aliases. The policy remains jump-to-11, taken-miss-to-10, saturating taken-hit increment, matching-only saturating not-taken decrement with retained target, and matching-only invalidation.

A shared valid/index/30-bit target record delays the existing indexed target-array write to the same edge as metadata commit. Both pending-valid paths refresh on every non-reset edge, independently of stalls and redirects. Reset cancels capture and commit and clears pending/table validity; masked payloads retain their values. Fetch sees committed state only and uses the pre-edge prediction on a commit edge. There is no training bypass, metadata snapshot, maintenance forwarding, or added architectural interlock. Immediate EX recovery, the exact prediction carried with each instruction, resolved RVFI next PC, nret=1, all external ports, and execution scheduling remain unchanged.

No architectural deviation from the hypothesis was needed. Source event state is exactly `16*(1+26+2) + (1+4+30) = 499` bits. Yosys automatically recodes each two-bit command into four state bits, so mapped event storage is 496 row flops plus 35 shared target flops, or 531 flops. The complete routed core gains 559 FFs after other synthesis/mapping differences.

The IF reference applies accepted events with an explicit one-edge delay and checks the public output bundle and fetch address before and after every checked edge. Coverage includes all rows, every tag and target bit, allocation, threshold crossings, saturation, target replacement/retention, illegal-control priority, not-taken misses, matching/nonmatching invalidations, simultaneous capture/commit, continuous aliases, idle draining, fetch stalls, recovery, flush, and reset with pending work. The existing deterministic 512-cycle random stream is retained, followed by probes of every exercised tag and each row's counter behavior.

The pipeline harness now checks predictions before and after every edge against an independent ordered policy model. It pairs accepted fetches with exactly one advancing-EX resolution, verifies recovery against the exact accepted prediction, and pairs retirements with those resolutions. Existing order, PC-chain, operand, arithmetic, trap, and wrong-path-store assertions remain. New directed tests cover pending commits during instruction stalls, memory holds, divide waits, younger redirects, and reset. Only two existing timing expectations changed: a cold self-jump now misses twice before sustaining one retirement per cycle, and immediate alternating aliases can sometimes hit the still-committed previous entry. Each recovery still kills exactly the existing younger slot and costs one bubble.

No live EX signal or another row's state reaches commit. All 416 pending-tag bits remain distinct across the sixteen rows; event capture has no table-state dependency. title: Bank-local registered training commands for the target predictor
motivation:
The current row-local predictor reaches 350.46 iter/s at 147.75 MHz,
with all three reported critical paths running from ID/EX resolve-PC
bits through local tag matching to metadata enables. The median path
is 6.77 ns, including 3.72 ns of routing. This makes training fanout
and placement a more evidenced opportunity than greater associativity:
hyp-20260905-003-r2s2 lost frequency with essentially unchanged cycles.
The delayed row-snapshot experiment hyp-20260905-002-r3s1 reached only

4,215,937 to 4,215,262. That supports a small feedback-latency budget,
without establishing that pipelining alone will improve this winner.
Bank-local command registers can isolate the current high-fanout
resolve-PC path while retaining its successful scalar metadata and
indexed target storage.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one cycle of predictor-training latency using four bank-local
registered command slots inside if_stage. Keep the existing sixteen
direct-mapped entries, PC[5:2] index, full PC[31:6] tags, aligned
target[31:2] values, and two-bit branch counters. Partition only the
metadata update circuitry into four groups of four consecutive rows:
resolve_pc[5:4] selects the bank and resolve_pc[3:2] selects its row.
Prediction policy, fetch lookup, instruction pipeline depth, and
architectural recovery latency retain their current definitions.

On edge N, accept the existing resolve_valid event. Each bank updates
its pending-valid bit every non-reset edge to resolve_valid AND its
bank-index match. The selected bank captures the full 26-bit tag,
a four-bit one-hot row selection, and legal/branch/jump/taken flags.
Give each bank payload its own bank-specific capture enable: these
registers retain distinct histories, allowing local placement and
limiting each registered command tag to four metadata rows. Capture
raw command fields, with no table-state read, tag comparison, or
counter calculation on this capture path. Existing resolve_valid
qualification remains authoritative for valid EX advancement through
memory holds and divide waits.

During the following cycle, each pending command compares its tag
with the addressed row's live scalar tag and computes that row's
next state. Commit on edge N+1. Keep the successful constant-index
valid/tag/counter registers and local saturation logic from r3s2.
The committed state from the preceding event is already visible to
the next event's calculation, including consecutive same-row updates
and different tags aliasing a row. Thus commands sustain one accepted
resolution per cycle and need neither captured metadata snapshots
nor maintenance forwarding. Every metadata update uses registered
bank command fields rather than live resolve_pc or resolve flags.

Keep the separate 16x30 indexed target array and its single synchronous
write port. Register its write index, target data, and qualified write
event alongside the bank commands, so a target write commits on the

implementation_notes:
Implemented the bank-local registered training hypothesis in `cores/bench/rtl/if_stage.sv`, with latency-aware reference and directed tests in `cores/bench/test/test_if_stage.py` and `cores/bench/test/test_pipeline.py`. Correctness gates pass. The measured scored fitness is **346.33671643660585 iter/s**, **1.1765347153438688% below 350.46**. The estimated four-percent gain was not realized.

Four command slots use resolve PC[5:4] to select their individual capture enables. Each retains a full 26-bit tag, four-bit one-hot PC[3:2] row selection, and raw legal/branch/jump/taken flags. Every non-reset edge refreshes each pending-valid bit, independently of IF stalls, memory holds, divide waits, flushes, and redirects. Payload registers capture only for their selected bank and otherwise retain their distinct histories. No table read, tag comparison, or counter calculation precedes capture.

On the following edge, the selected constant-index scalar metadata row commits against its live valid/tag/counter state. Consecutive commands therefore observe preceding commits without snapshots or forwarding. The original transition policy is retained: jumps allocate/update to 11; taken branches allocate 10 on a miss or saturating-increment a hit; not-taken branches decrement only a hit and retain its target; non-control or illegal/trapping resolutions invalidate only a matching tag. Unselected rows retain state.

The separate 16x30 indexed target array retains one synchronous write port. An independent registered write event, four-bit index, and 30-bit target commit on the matching metadata edge. Target payload capture is enabled only for an accepted legal jump or taken legal branch. Reset has priority over both capture and commit, clears all table valid bits and pending-valid/write-event bits, and leaves unused payloads unreset. The declaration adds 175 command-state bits; implementation optimization produces a net increase of 172 device FFs.

Fetch uses committed state only. A fetch accepted on either the capture edge or the following commit edge uses its pre-edge prediction, with no pending-command bypass. Instruction pipeline depth, recovery priority, accepted-prediction capture, EX architectural-next-PC comparison, resolve_valid qualification, RVFI reporting, decoder legality, nret=1, all external ports, divider, and ALTOPS behavior are unchanged. No architectural deviation from the hypothesis was needed.

The independent reference model carries one ordered raw command, applies it one edge after acceptance against current model state, and checks the complete public IF output bundle and fetch address before and after each edge. It does not inspect DUT metadata or command registers. Coverage includes all sixteen rows and four banks, consecutive same-row increments/decrements, both saturation limits, alias replacement and invalidation, interleaved banks, target/metadata atomicity, every tag and stored target bit, PC wraparound, fetch/training collisions, bubbles, idle/stall/flush/redirect draining, and reset with pending and concurrently offered commands.

Pipeline traces also check those public IF outputs against the same delayed reference before and after every edge. Four new directed tests exercise pending commits during imem backpressure, invalidation from an advancing load during its subsequent older-memory hold, divide waits, a younger redirect, and reset immediately before commit in each bank. Existing held-EX, forwarded-operand, RVFI order/PC-chain, links, trap, changing-JALR, stale-code, wrong-path retirement/store, and real divider checks remain. Only latency-dependent expectations changed: cold self-jumps miss twice before warm one-retirement-per-cycle execution, and alternating full-tag aliases can hit the older resident entry before its pending replacement commits. The alias test still requires full-width destinations and recovery matching the exact accepted prediction.

title: Remove wide ID/EX payload registers from bubble-control fanout
motivation:
The current winner, hyp-20260905-002-r4s1, scores 371.55 iter/s at
156.62 MHz median Fmax. Its median-seed timing report identifies a
6.39 ns path from predicted_next_pc[0], through prediction recovery
and hazard/divide qualification, to an ID/EX operand register RESET.
The final control net alone contributes 1.95 ns of routing. In the
current RTL, reset || flush clears the entire id_ex_t payload, and
stall_id also includes the load-use condition even though that case
inserts a bubble. Recovery therefore controls many data-register
reset/enable pins whose values cannot matter for a killed instruction.

Prior micro_opt attempts rewrote register-file selection, ALU operation
selection, and predictor training/tag comparisons; none isolated ID/EX
bubble controls from payload storage. LESSONS.md records that the ALU
rewrite exposed this recovery path, while forced predictor comparison
boundaries regressed timing. The latest winner has already registered
predictor training events. A local rewrite of bubble insertion now
targets a measured control-distribution bottleneck without changing
predictor policy, arithmetic, or architectural scheduling.
